title: Unary Isotope Variations Before Collapse
body:
Unary isotope variation is the narrowest kind of atom-type variation: the same element, differing only in neutron count and therefore in mass. Hydrogen, deuterium, and tritium are the famous trio, but the class also covers carbon-12 and carbon-13, oxygen-16 and oxygen-18, lithium-6 and lithium-7, boron-10 and boron-11, and silicon-28, 29, and 30. Because isotopes share the same electron count, their chemistry is nearly identical, which makes them the cleanest possible mixture: any difference in behavior comes from mass alone, through vibration frequencies, diffusion speeds, and zero-point energy, rather than from different bonding.

Variation class. This record covers the unary isotope variation class: one element at a time, varied only by isotope. Its atom types are hydrogen, deuterium, and tritium; carbon-12 and carbon-13; oxygen-16 and oxygen-18; lithium-6 and lithium-7; boron-10 and boron-11; and silicon-28, silicon-29, and silicon-30. No second element enters this class, which is what makes it unary: the variation is mass variation inside a single element, and every mixture in the class is a blend of isotopes of that element in some proportion.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are mass-scaling vibrational analysis and the diffusion isotope effect. Vibrational frequencies scale with the inverse square root of mass, so replacing an isotope shifts every vibration by a computable fraction, and the shift is largest for hydrogen, where doubling the mass is a large relative change. Diffusion speeds scale the same way for light atoms, so isotope blends separate measurably under a gradient, which is the basis of isotope separation. The demo computes the vibrational shift for hydrogen-deuterium, carbon-12/13, and oxygen-16/18 from their masses.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for unary isotope variations before collapse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: H/D: vibrational shift 29.3%; C-12/13: vibrational shift 3.9%; O-16/18: vibrational shift 5.7%; ENDPOINT: isotope effects strongest for H/D (29.3%); quantum regime below Debye temperature Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Stability range. The stability range for isotope variations is essentially the whole composition range at ordinary temperatures: isotopes of one element mix in all proportions, because their bonding is identical and no chemical driving force separates them. The range holds from cryogenic temperatures up to the element's melting and boiling points, and the only variation inside it is the size of the isotope effect itself, which shrinks as temperature rises and thermal energy swamps the mass differences.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is not a phase split but the disappearance of isotope identity as a useful distinction. Above the element's Debye temperature, thermal motion washes out zero-point differences and isotope effects become small corrections rather than deciding factors. At the other extreme, the class stops being possible when the element itself leaves the condensed state: a vaporized or ionized element no longer holds the mixture the class describes. The demo's endpoint states the hydrogen-deuterium shift, the largest in the class, as the threshold marker.

Use and limits. Use this record when isotope blends matter, such as tracing water sources by oxygen ratios, dating by carbon ratios, or separating lithium isotopes, and as the unary anchor of the whole variation partition. Do not use it where a second element enters, because that mixture belongs to a higher-arity class, and do not treat model shifts as measured spectra, because real spectra need full quantum calculations. title: Binary Mixture Architectures Before Collapse
body:
Binary mixture architecture is the two-type variation class: every mixture in it blends exactly two atom types, A and B, in some proportion from pure A to pure B. Binary mixtures are the workhorse of alloy science, because two types already produce the full drama of mixing: complete mixing, partial mixing with a miscibility gap, compound formation, and ordering, all controlled by one composition variable and temperature. Classic examples include copper-nickel, which mixes completely, and iron-copper, which largely refuses to mix, and the same two-type frame describes gas mixtures, liquid pairs, and solid solutions alike.

Variation class. This record covers the binary mixture architecture class: mixtures of exactly two atom types, with no third type present. Its atom types are written generically as A and B, because the class is defined by count, not by chemistry: any pair of elements, from copper-nickel to iron-copper to argon-krypton, belongs here when only those two types are present. Chemistry-specific binary families, such as alkali pairs or halogen pairs, are cross-referenced from their family classes, while this record governs the two-type architecture itself.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the regular solution model, Metropolis Monte Carlo swaps, and the CALPHAD common-tangent construction. The regular solution model gives the free-energy curve and its spinodal points in closed form. Monte Carlo swaps watch the mixture separate or stay mixed under the Metropolis rule. The common tangent gives the equilibrium pair of compositions when the mixture does split. The demo uses the regular solution model with a teaching interaction strength of ten thousand joules per mole.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for binary mixture architectures before collapse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: interaction Omega: 10000 J/mol; critical temperature Tc: 601 K; at 298 K: chi=4.04, spinodal x=0.1449 and x=0.8551; ENDPOINT: mixture splits between x=0.1449 and x=0.8551 at 298 K; single mixture above Tc=601 K Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Stability range. The stability range for binary mixtures is temperature-dependent: above the critical temperature, entropy wins and the two types mix in all proportions as a single phase. Below it, a miscibility gap opens, and only compositions outside the gap stay single-phase, while compositions inside split into the gap's two edge compositions. The range is therefore stated as a temperature window, not a fixed composition list, and the window's width is set by the interaction strength.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is the critical temperature, where the spinodal points meet and the miscibility gap closes, together with the spinodal compositions at any working temperature. Below the critical temperature, the mixed state inside the gap collapses by spinodal decomposition or nucleation into two phases. The demo computes the critical temperature and the spinodal compositions at room temperature, and its endpoint states both as the class threshold.

Use and limits. Use this record for any two-type mixture question, as the arity anchor for all binary families, and as the template for ternary and higher architectures. Do not use the teaching interaction strength as a measured value for a real pair, because real pairs need fitted or computed interactions. title: Noble-Gas Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
Noble-gas mixtures are the most peaceable variation class: the group-18 elements, helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, and radon, have full outer electron shells and no chemical appetite, so they mix as gases without reacting, forming compounds, or ordering. Their mixtures are governed by weak dispersion forces, which the Lennard-Jones model captures well, and their behavior is close to ideal at ordinary pressures. Noble-gas mixtures matter for lighting, for cryogenics, for breathing gases, and as the textbook example of mixing driven by entropy alone, because nothing else interferes.

Variation class. This record covers the noble-gas family class: mixtures whose atom types all come from group 18. Its atom types are helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, and radon. No reactive element enters this class, which is what makes it the inert end of the variation partition: where the reactive classes collapse by compound formation, this class has no compounds to collapse into, and its limits come from physics alone.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the Lorentz-Berthelot combining rules for cross interactions, the virial equation for gas behavior, and Lennard-Jones molecular dynamics for liquid mixtures. The combining rules give cross energy depths and sizes from pure values. The virial equation corrects ideal-gas behavior at higher pressures. Molecular dynamics follows liquid mixtures directly. The demo computes the argon-krypton cross pair from textbook pure values.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for noble-gas mixtures before collapse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: eps_Ar: 120.0 K; eps_Kr: 170.0 K; eps_AB (Lorentz-Berthelot): 142.83 K; sigma_AB (Lorentz-Berthelot): 3.525 A; ENDPOINT: Ar-Kr cross pair defined, eps_AB=142.83 K, sigma_AB=3.525 A Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Stability range. The stability range for noble-gas mixtures is broad: as gases they mix in all proportions at all ordinary temperatures and pressures, because entropy favors mixing and no interaction opposes it. As liquids at cryogenic temperatures they also mix broadly, with only small deviations from ideality. The range covers every composition from pure helium to pure radon, limited at the top by temperature and pressure rather than by chemistry.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is condensation and freezing, not phase separation: below the mixture's critical temperature the gas collapses into a liquid, and below its freezing point into a solid, and at very high pressure the mixture can separate into denser and lighter fluid regions. The demo's endpoint states the argon-krypton cross pair, the input every noble-gas mixture calculation needs, and the class threshold is the critical temperature of the mixture, below which the single gas phase ceases to exist.

Use and limits. Use this record for breathing gases, lighting fills, cryogenic mixtures, and as the inert reference for the whole partition. Do not use it for reactive mixtures, and do not treat textbook Lennard-Jones values as exact, because real noble-gas interactions need fitted potentials. title: Alkali Metal Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
Alkali metal mixtures are the group-1 variation class: lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, and cesium, the softest and most reactive metals, each with a single outer electron it gives up readily. As liquids, alkali metals mix broadly, which is why liquid sodium-potassium coolant and liquid lithium blankets are real engineering materials. As solids, their mixing is limited by size: lithium is much smaller than cesium, so their crystal lattices strain when forced together, and the strain sets the solid solubility. The class is reactive throughout, so its mixtures must be kept from air, water, and other reactive partners, or the mixture collapses by reaction rather than by separation.

Variation class. This record covers the alkali family class: mixtures whose atom types all come from group 1. Its atom types are lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, and cesium. No other family enters this class, which keeps it disjoint from the alkaline-earth, transition-metal, and other family classes: a mixture belongs here exactly when all its types are alkali metals.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the regular solution model for miscibility gaps, the Miedema model for semi-empirical heats of mixing, and the Hume-Rothery size rule for solid solubility. The regular solution model gives the critical temperature from a teaching interaction strength. The Miedema model estimates heats of mixing from electron density and electronegativity. The size rule flags pairs whose radii differ by more than fifteen percent. The demo uses the regular solution model with a teaching interaction strength of six thousand joules per mole.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for alkali metal mixtures before collapse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: interaction Omega: 6000 J/mol; critical temperature Tc: 361 K; at 298 K: chi=2.42, spinodal x=0.2913 and x=0.7087; ENDPOINT: mixture splits between x=0.2913 and x=0.7087 at 298 K; single mixture above Tc=361 K Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Stability range. The stability range for alkali mixtures is wide as liquids and narrow as solids. Liquid alkali pairs mix in all proportions above their critical temperatures, which for weakly interacting pairs sit near or below room temperature. Solid solutions exist only where sizes are close, notably sodium-potassium and potassium-rubidium, while lithium pairs with the heavier alkalis split on cooling. The range is therefore stated as a liquid window plus a solid window, not a single list.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is the critical temperature of the liquid miscibility gap together with the fifteen-percent size rule for solids. Below the critical temperature, a liquid mixture inside the gap collapses into two liquids; in the solid, a pair failing the size rule collapses into separate crystals or into an intermetallic compound. The demo computes the critical temperature and the room-temperature spinodal for its teaching interaction, and its endpoint states both.

Do not use the teaching interaction strength as a measured value, and do not handle alkali metals without their safety procedures, which this record describes but does not replace. title: Alkaline-Earth Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
Alkaline-earth mixtures are the group-2 variation class: beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, and barium, each with two outer electrons and a reactivity below the alkalis but above most metals. Magnesium alloys are the class's most important members, used where light weight matters, and calcium and strontium appear as alloying additions and as modifiers. The family spans a wide size range, from small beryllium to large barium, so size mismatch governs much of its mixing: neighbors in the group mix more readily than distant cousins, and the Hume-Rothery fifteen-percent rule predicts the pattern well.

Variation class. This record covers the alkaline-earth family class: mixtures whose atom types all come from group 2. Its atom types are beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, and barium. The class is disjoint from the alkali class by group membership: a mixture belongs here exactly when all its types are alkaline-earth metals, with magnesium as the usual solvent and reference.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the Hume-Rothery size rule, the regular solution model, and the CALPHAD common tangent. The size rule compares each member's radius against magnesium and flags pairs beyond fifteen percent. The regular solution model gives miscibility gaps from interaction strengths. The common tangent gives equilibrium phase pairs when a mixture splits. The demo applies the size rule against magnesium with model radii stated in the record.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for alkaline-earth mixtures before collapse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: Be: mismatch vs Mg 30.0% COLLAPSE-RISK; Mg: mismatch vs Mg 0.0% PASS; Ca: mismatch vs Mg 23.1% COLLAPSE-RISK; Sr: mismatch vs Mg 34.4% COLLAPSE-RISK; Ba: mismatch vs Mg 38.8% COLLAPSE-RISK; ENDPOINT: Hume-Rothery 15% rule vs Mg; pairs above 15%% collapse out of solid solution Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Stability range. The stability range for alkaline-earth mixtures is set by size and structure: pairs within fifteen percent of the solvent form broad solid solutions, while distant pairs have narrow ranges or split into separate phases. Magnesium-calcium and magnesium-strontium mix usefully, while beryllium pairs are restricted by its small size and barium pairs by its large size. The range is therefore stated per pair, not as a single window, and the demo's table is the range.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is the fifteen-percent size mismatch: beyond it, substitutional solid solution collapses and the mixture splits into separate crystals or into intermetallic compounds. Temperature softens the rule somewhat, because entropy at high temperature tolerates more strain, but the threshold remains the working boundary for solid mixing. The demo's endpoint states which members pass and which fail against magnesium.

Use and limits. Use this record for magnesium alloy design, for alkaline-earth additions, and as the group-2 anchor of the family partition. Do not use model radii as exact crystal radii, because radii depend on coordination and charge state, and do not use the size rule alone where compounds form. title: Light-Element Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
Light-element mixtures are the low-atomic-number variation class: every element up to neon, hydrogen through neon, spanning gases, reactive nonmetals, and the lightest metals. This class is defined by mass and size, not by group, so it cuts across the family classes: it holds the lightest member of several families at once. Light mixtures matter out of proportion to their size, because they include water chemistry, organic chemistry, hydrogen storage, and the lightest structural materials, and because their small atoms diffuse fast, react readily, and show the largest quantum effects.

Variation class. This record covers the light-element range class: mixtures whose atom types all have atomic number ten or below. Its atom types are hydrogen, helium, lithium, beryllium, boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, and neon. The class is defined by its atomic-number ceiling, which keeps it disjoint from the heavy-element range class: a mixture belongs here exactly when every type sits at or below neon.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the Hume-Rothery size rule, electronegativity difference analysis, and the regular solution model. The size rule tests whether two light atoms can share a lattice. Electronegativity differences predict whether a pair will compound instead of mixing, which for light elements is the common outcome. The regular solution model gives miscibility gaps where mixing survives. The demo applies the size rule against lithium with model radii.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for light-element mixtures before collapse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Stability range. The stability range for light-element mixtures is narrow for solids and broad for gases. Light gases mix readily, but light solids rarely form broad substitutional solutions, because their radii span a wide range and their bonding differs sharply: hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine prefer molecules and compounds over shared lattices. The range is therefore stated as broad for gas mixtures and narrow for solid solutions, with compounds as the usual stable outcome.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is twofold: the fifteen-percent size rule for solid solutions, and the compound-formation threshold for reactive pairs, where a compound's formation energy beats the mixing energy and the mixture collapses into the compound. Most light pairs cross one threshold or the other, which is why the demo's table shows many failures: the class's honest result is that light atoms usually compound or stay gaseous rather than sharing a crystal. The demo's endpoint states the size-rule verdicts.

Do not use model radii as exact values, and do not expect broad solid solutions among light elements without checking compound formation first. title: Immiscible and Weakly Interacting Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
Immiscible mixtures are the behavior class defined by refusal: pairs whose unlike interactions cost so much energy that the mixture would rather split than stir. Classic pairs include iron-copper, silver-nickel, copper-lead, and tungsten-copper, all used precisely because they stay separate, whether as bearing alloys, as electrical composites, or as infiltrated structures. Immiscibility is not a failure of mixing but a property to use, and the class exists so that refusal is catalogued as carefully as acceptance: knowing what will not mix is as useful as knowing what will.

Variation class. This record covers the immiscible behavior class: mixtures whose defining trait is a large positive heat of mixing, whatever their families. Its example atom types are iron, copper, silver, nickel, lead, aluminum, and tungsten, in pairs such as iron-copper, silver-nickel, and copper-lead. The class is defined by behavior, not by group: a pair belongs here when its interaction strength is large enough to open a wide miscibility gap, and the same pair may also appear in its family class for other purposes.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the regular solution model with a large interaction strength, Metropolis Monte Carlo swaps, and the CALPHAD common tangent. The regular solution model gives the wide gap and high critical temperature directly. Monte Carlo swaps watch the mixed state collapse into domains. The common tangent gives the equilibrium pair compositions. The demo uses the regular solution model with a teaching interaction strength of twenty thousand joules per mole.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for immiscible and weakly interacting mixtures before collapse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: interaction Omega: 20000 J/mol; critical temperature Tc: 1203 K; at 298 K: chi=8.07, spinodal x=0.0663 and x=0.9337; ENDPOINT: mixture splits between x=0.0663 and x=0.9337 at 298 K; single mixture above Tc=1203 K Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Stability range. The stability range for immiscible mixtures is narrow as a single phase and wide as a two-phase composite. Single-phase stability exists only at high temperature, above the critical temperature, or in dilute corners where one type dissolves slightly in the other. Everywhere else, the stable state is two phases side by side, and the range is stated as the dilute solubilities plus the high-temperature window, not as a broad middle.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is the critical temperature together with the room-temperature spinodal: below the critical temperature, any composition inside the gap collapses into the two edge compositions, and the gap at room temperature is nearly the whole range for strongly immiscible pairs. The demo computes the critical temperature and the room-temperature spinodal for its teaching interaction, and its endpoint states both as the class threshold.

Use and limits. Use this record to choose bearing pairs, composites, and infiltrated structures, and as the refusal anchor of the behavior partition. Do not use the teaching interaction strength as a measured value, and do not force an immiscible pair into a single phase without a process, such as rapid quenching, that traps it there. title: Halogen Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
Halogen mixtures are the group-17 variation class: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine, the most reactive nonmetals, each one electron short of a full shell. Halogens mix with each other readily as gases and liquids, but their mixtures are restless: they form interhalogen compounds such as chlorine fluoride and iodine chloride, and the line between a mixture and a compound is thin. Fluorine is the extreme member, reacting with nearly everything, while iodine is the gentlest, and the class's behavior runs from violent to mild across its four members.

Variation class. This record covers the halogen family class: mixtures whose atom types all come from group 17. Its atom types are fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine. Astatine, the fifth halogen, is left out of the enumeration deliberately, because it is so rare and short-lived that no practical mixture of it exists: the class covers the halogens that can actually be mixed. A mixture belongs here exactly when all its types are halogens.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are compound-formation energetics, interhalogen stability rules, and the regular solution model. Formation energetics compare each interhalogen compound's energy against the mixing energy, deciding whether the mixture survives or collapses into the compound. Stability rules predict which interhalogens exist from size and electronegativity patterns. The regular solution model covers the rare cases where halogens mix without compounding. The demo compares model formation energies against model mixing energies for three interhalogens.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for halogen mixtures before collapse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Stability range. The stability range for halogen mixtures is the gas and liquid range where no compound wins: halogen gases mix readily at ordinary temperatures when no compound formation is favored, and liquid bromine-iodine mixtures persist where interhalogens do not dominate. The range narrows sharply where a stable interhalogen exists, because the compound then claims the composition. The range is therefore stated per pair, with compound-dominated pairs excluded from the mixture range.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is the compound-formation threshold: when an interhalogen compound's formation energy falls below the mixing energy, the mixture collapses into the compound, and no mixture of the original halogens survives at that composition. Fluorine pairs cross the threshold most readily, iodine pairs least. The demo's endpoint states which model pairs compound and which survive as mixtures.

title: Ternary Mixture Architectures Before Collapse
body:
Ternary mixture architecture is the three-type variation class: every mixture in it blends exactly three atom types, which adds a composition triangle in place of the binary line and opens behaviors no binary mixture can show. Three types allow two-phase regions with tie lines, three-phase triangles, and ordered ternary compounds, and the composition space itself becomes two-dimensional, so a ternary phase diagram is a map rather than a curve. Ternary mixtures include stainless steels, brasses with a third addition, and semiconductor alloys tuned by two independent compositions at once.

Variation class. This record covers the ternary mixture architecture class: mixtures of exactly three atom types, with no fourth type present. Its atom types are written generically as A, B, and C, because the class is defined by count: any three elements, from iron-chromium-nickel to gallium-arsenic-phosphorus, belong here when only those three types are present. Chemistry-specific ternary families are cross-referenced from their family classes, while this record governs the three-type architecture itself.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are configurational entropy analysis, the regular solution model extended to three components, and CALPHAD ternary isotherms. Entropy analysis gives the ideal mixing entropy for three types, which exceeds the binary value and stabilizes ternaries against splitting. The three-component regular solution model gives spinodal surfaces from three pair interactions. CALPHAD isotherms map the resulting phase regions. The demo computes the ternary configurational entropy and the entropy-stabilization temperature for a teaching enthalpy.

The range is therefore stated as a temperature window plus a composition triangle, not a single interval, and the demo's stabilization temperature marks the window's floor.

Collapse threshold. Below the threshold, the ternary mixture collapses into two or three phases along tie lines or into a three-phase triangle. The demo computes the stabilization temperature for a teaching enthalpy and its endpoint states it as the class threshold.

title: Post-Transition Metal Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
Post-transition metal mixtures are the soft-metal variation class: aluminum, gallium, indium, tin, thallium, lead, and bismuth, the metals that follow the transition block and behave more like soft, low-melting materials than like steels. Their mixtures include solders, fusible alloys, and bearing metals, and their low melting points make them the class where liquid mixing is easiest to reach: several pairs melt below the boiling point of water, and bismuth alloys can melt in a warm room. The class spans a wide size range, so size mismatch still governs solid mixing, but liquid mixing is the class's natural state.

Variation class. This record covers the post-transition family class: mixtures whose atom types all come from the post-transition metals. Its atom types are aluminum, gallium, indium, tin, thallium, lead, and bismuth. The class is disjoint from the transition-metal class by block position: a mixture belongs here exactly when all its types are post-transition metals, with aluminum or tin as the usual solvent.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the Hume-Rothery size rule, the regular solution model, and eutectic analysis. The size rule tests solid solubility against the solvent. The regular solution model gives miscibility gaps from interaction strengths. Eutectic analysis locates the low-melting compositions where two phases freeze together, which is the class's most useful feature. The demo applies the size rule against aluminum with model radii.

title: Metalloid Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
Metalloid mixtures are the in-between variation class: boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, and tellurium, the elements that sit on the staircase between metals and nonmetals and share properties of both. Metalloid mixtures matter for electronics, thermoelectrics, and photonics, where composition tunes the band gap, and their collapse modes include ordering, compound formation, and band-edge shifts that change the material's character before any phase splits.

Its atom types are boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, and tellurium. title: Carbon-Group Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
Carbon-group mixtures are the group-14 vertical class: carbon, silicon, germanium, tin, and lead, the elements that share four outer electrons and run from the hardest nonmetal to soft metals down the group. Their mixtures include silicon-germanium, the canonical semiconductor alloy, and tin-lead solders, and their behavior changes down the group as bonding shifts from covalent to metallic. Carbon itself mixes little in this family, because diamond's rigidity rejects substitutes, while silicon and germanium mix completely and tin and lead mix as soft metals.

Variation class. This record covers the carbon-group family class: mixtures whose atom types all come from group 14. Its atom types are carbon, silicon, germanium, tin, and lead. The class is disjoint from the other group families by group membership: a mixture belongs here exactly when all its types are group-14 elements, with silicon or germanium as the usual solvent.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are Vegard's law for lattice spacing, the regular solution model for miscibility gaps, and semiconductor alloy theory for band-gap bowing. Vegard's law interpolates lattice spacing linearly with composition. The regular solution model gives gaps from interaction strengths. Alloy theory tracks the band gap's bend with composition. The demo applies Vegard's law to silicon-germanium across the full composition range.

title: Oxygen-Group Mixtures Before Collapse

Oxygen-group mixtures are the group-16 vertical class: oxygen, sulfur, selenium, and tellurium, the chalcogens, each two electrons short of a full shell and strongly inclined to take them. title: Compound-Forming Reactive Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
Compound-forming reactive mixtures are the behavior class defined by chemistry winning over mixing: pairs whose reaction into a compound releases so much energy that no mixture of the original types survives. Alkali metals with halogens, alkaline earths with oxygen or sulfur, and similar pairs belong here, and their compounds, lithium fluoride, sodium chloride, magnesium oxide, calcium sulfide, are among the most stable materials known. The class exists so that reaction is catalogued as a collapse mode in its own right, distinct from phase separation: where immiscible pairs split into two mixtures, reactive pairs vanish into a compound.

Variation class. This record covers the reactive compound-forming behavior class: mixtures whose defining trait is a strongly negative compound-formation energy. Its example atom types are lithium, fluorine, sodium, chlorine, magnesium, oxygen, calcium, and sulfur, in pairs such as lithium-fluorine, sodium-chlorine, magnesium-oxygen, and calcium-sulfur. The class is defined by behavior, not by group: a pair belongs here when its compound's formation energy beats the mixing energy by a wide margin, whatever families the pair comes from.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are compound-formation energetics, electronegativity difference analysis, and CALPHAD compound equilibria. Formation energetics compare each compound's energy against the mixing energy. Electronegativity differences predict which pairs react strongly, since large differences mean electron transfer and ionic bonding. CALPHAD equilibria place the compound in the full phase diagram. The demo compares model formation energies against model mixing energies for four reactive pairs.

title: Quaternary Mixture Architectures Before Collapse
body:
Quaternary mixture architecture is the four-type variation class: every mixture in it blends exactly four atom types, which adds a composition tetrahedron in place of the ternary triangle and opens four-phase equilibria and ordered quaternary compounds. Four types allow independent tuning of several properties at once, which is why quaternary mixtures include advanced steels, superalloys with several additions, and quaternary semiconductors such as copper-zinc-tin-sulfide. The composition space is three-dimensional, so a quaternary phase diagram is a volume, and its sections, not its whole, are what engineers read.

Variation class. This record covers the quaternary mixture architecture class: mixtures of exactly four atom types, with no fifth type present. Its atom types are written generically as A, B, C, and D, because the class is defined by count: any four elements belong here when only those four types are present. Chemistry-specific quaternary families are cross-referenced from their family classes, while this record governs the four-type architecture itself.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are configurational entropy analysis, the regular solution model extended to four components, and CALPHAD multicomponent equilibria. Entropy analysis gives the ideal mixing entropy for four types, which exceeds the ternary value and further stabilizes the single phase. The four-component regular solution model gives spinodal volumes from six pair interactions. CALPHAD equilibria map the resulting phase volumes. The demo computes the quaternary configurational entropy and the entropy-stabilization temperature for a teaching enthalpy.

title: High-Entropy Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
High-entropy mixtures are the five-or-more-type variation class: mixtures that blend five or more atom types in near-equal proportions, so that configurational entropy becomes a leading force rather than a correction. The class includes high-entropy alloys such as iron-cobalt-nickel-chromium-manganese, the Cantor alloy, and high-entropy ceramics, where five or more cations share a lattice. The defining idea is that entropy can stabilize a single disordered phase where enthalpy alone would split the mixture, and the class's threshold is the temperature where that stabilization takes over.

Variation class. This record covers the high-entropy architecture class: mixtures of five or more atom types in near-equal proportions. Its example atom types are iron, cobalt, nickel, chromium, manganese, aluminum, and copper, in combinations of five or more. The class is defined by count and by proportion: a mixture belongs here when it holds five or more types near equally, and dilute additions to a four-type base do not qualify.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are configurational entropy analysis, the high-entropy stabilization criterion, and CALPHAD multicomponent equilibria. Entropy analysis gives the mixing entropy for five or more types, which reaches and exceeds thirteen joules per mole-kelvin. The stabilization criterion compares the entropy term against the enthalpy term at a working temperature. CALPHAD equilibria map the resulting single-phase fields. The demo computes entropies for one through six types and the stabilization temperature for a five-type teaching enthalpy.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for high-entropy mixtures before collapse. Stability range. The stability range for high-entropy mixtures is the high-temperature window where entropy wins: above the stabilization temperature, the single disordered phase is stable across a broad composition region, while below it, the mixture splits or orders. The range is therefore stated as a temperature window plus a near-equimolar composition region, and the window's floor is the demo's stabilization temperature.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is the stabilization temperature: below it, entropy stops outweighing enthalpy and the high-entropy mixture collapses into multiple phases or into an ordered compound. The threshold rises with enthalpy and falls with type count, which is why adding types helps only when the added types do not raise the enthalpy too much. title: Transition-Metal Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
Transition-metal mixtures are the largest variation class in the partition: the d-block elements, from scandium to mercury across three rows, whose partially filled d-shells give them their strength, magnetism, color, and catalytic power. Their mixtures include steels, superalloys, brasses, bronzes, and coinage alloys, which is to say most of the metal world. Transition metals mix broadly among neighbors, because their sizes and structures are close, and narrowly with distant members, because size and structure diverge, and the class's map is essentially the map of metallurgy.

Variation class. This record covers the transition-metal family class: mixtures whose atom types all come from the d-block. Its atom types are scandium, titanium, vanadium, chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel, copper, zinc, yttrium, zirconium, niobium, molybdenum, technetium, ruthenium, rhodium, palladium, silver, cadmium, hafnium, tantalum, tungsten, rhenium, osmium, iridium, platinum, gold, and mercury. title: Lanthanide Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
Lanthanide mixtures are the rare-earth variation class: lanthanum through lutetium, the fifteen elements whose f-shells fill across the row and whose chemistry is famously similar. Their mixtures include mischmetal, the mixed rare-earth alloy used in lighters and steels, and neodymium-iron-boron magnet alloys, where a lanthanide mixture tunes the magnet. The class's signature is the lanthanide contraction: radii shrink steadily across the row, but by so little that neighbors are nearly the same size, which makes lanthanide mixing unusually broad.

Variation class. This record covers the lanthanide family class: mixtures whose atom types all come from the lanthanide row. Its atom types are lanthanum, cerium, praseodymium, neodymium, promethium, samarium, europium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, holmium, erbium, thulium, ytterbium, and lutetium. The class is disjoint from the other families by row membership: a mixture belongs here exactly when all its types are lanthanides, with gadolinium as the middle reference.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the Hume-Rothery size rule, lanthanide contraction analysis, and rare-earth magnet alloy theory. The size rule tests solid solubility against gadolinium. Contraction analysis tracks the steady radius shrink across the row. Magnet theory tracks how mixed lanthanides tune anisotropy and Curie temperature. The demo applies the size rule against gadolinium with model radii for the full row.

title: Heavy-Element Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
Heavy-element mixtures are the high-atomic-number variation class: hafnium through bismuth, the dense metals whose weight, melting points, and radiation shielding set them apart. Their mixtures include tungsten heavy alloys, platinum-group alloys, and lead-bismuth coolants, and their behavior is governed by large masses, strong spin-orbit effects, and high densities. The class is defined by an atomic-number floor, so it cuts across the family classes: it holds the heaviest members of several families at once, and its collapse modes include pressure-driven structural collapse, where squeezing forces one crystal structure to give way to a denser one.

Variation class. This record covers the heavy-element range class: mixtures whose atom types all have atomic number seventy-two or above, capped at bismuth. Its atom types are hafnium, tantalum, tungsten, rhenium, osmium, iridium, platinum, gold, mercury, thallium, lead, and bismuth. The class is defined by its atomic-number floor and its bismuth cap, which keeps it disjoint from the light-element range class: a mixture belongs here exactly when every type sits between hafnium and bismuth inclusive.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the Birch-Murnaghan equation of state, the Hume-Rothery size rule, and high-pressure phase theory. The equation of state gives energy as a function of volume for each structure. The size rule tests solid solubility. High-pressure theory compares enthalpies across structures to find where one gives way to another. The demo compares a model crystal structure against a model dense structure and finds their enthalpy crossing.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for heavy-element mixtures before collapse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: collapse pressure: 0.0530 eV/A^3 = 8.5 GPa; ENDPOINT: dense structure wins above 8.5 GPa; open structure collapses Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Stability range. The stability range for heavy-element mixtures is broad at ordinary pressure for neighbors and narrow for distant pairs, and it narrows further under pressure, because squeezing favors the densest structure regardless of mixing. Tungsten-rhenium and platinum-iridium mix broadly, while lead-bismuth forms a eutectic coolant. The range is therefore stated as a pressure window plus per-pair solubilities, not a single interval.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is the pressure where the dense structure's enthalpy falls below the open structure's enthalpy, together with the fifteen-percent size rule for solid solutions. Beyond the pressure threshold, the mixture's structure collapses into the denser phase, and beyond the size limit, it splits into separate crystals. At the far limit of the class, documented single-atom physics sets an absolute ceiling: a point nucleus cannot bind its innermost electron beyond a critical charge near one hundred thirty-seven, and a finite nucleus extends the limit near one hundred seventy-three, which is why no stable mixture can include elements beyond the known table. The demo's endpoint states the structural collapse pressure for its model pair.

Use and limits. Use this record for heavy alloys, shielding, coolants, and as the high-mass anchor of the range partition. Do not use model equation-of-state parameters as measured values, and do not extrapolate the single-atom charge limit into mixture design, because it bounds elements, not alloys. title: Hydrogen-Bearing Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
Hydrogen-bearing mixtures are the special variation class where the smallest atom enters a host lattice: hydrogen dissolved in palladium, iron, titanium, zirconium, magnesium, or nickel, and the hydrides those mixtures form. Hydrogen is unique among mixture partners, because it is small enough to sit in the gaps between host atoms rather than replacing them, because it diffuses faster than any other element, and because its presence changes the host's strength, sometimes catastrophically, through embrittlement. The class matters for hydrogen storage, for fuel cells, and for the safety of hydrogen pipelines and pressure vessels.

Variation class. This record covers the hydrogen-bearing special class: mixtures of hydrogen with a host metal. Its atom types are hydrogen, palladium, iron, titanium, zirconium, magnesium, and nickel, in pairs or groups where hydrogen is the dissolved partner and the metal is the host. The class is defined by hydrogen's interstitial role, which keeps it disjoint from substitutional families: a mixture belongs here exactly when hydrogen enters the gaps of a host lattice rather than replacing host atoms.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are Sievert's law, hydride formation analysis, and hydrogen embrittlement theory. Sievert's law gives dissolved hydrogen concentration as proportional to the square root of hydrogen pressure. Hydride analysis compares the dissolved state against the hydride compound's stability. Embrittlement theory tracks how dissolved hydrogen lowers fracture resistance. The demo applies Sievert's law with a teaching constant and a teaching hydride threshold.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for hydrogen-bearing mixtures before collapse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: p=0.01 bar: dissolved H=0.002 dissolved; p=0.10 bar: dissolved H=0.006 dissolved; p=1.00 bar: dissolved H=0.020 dissolved; p=10.00 bar: dissolved H=0.063 dissolved; p=25.00 bar: dissolved H=0.100 HYDRIDE; ENDPOINT: hydride collapse threshold p*=25.0 bar at model K Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Stability range. The stability range for hydrogen-bearing mixtures is the dissolved window: below the hydride threshold concentration, hydrogen stays dissolved and the host keeps its structure, while the window's width depends on the host, with palladium dissolving the most and iron the least at ordinary pressure. The range is therefore stated as a pressure window per host, from trace dissolution up to the hydride threshold, and the demo's threshold pressure marks the window's top for its teaching parameters.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is the hydride threshold concentration: beyond it, the dissolved mixture collapses into a hydride phase, which is brittle and often cracks the host, and the collapse is the embrittlement failure mode that hydrogen safety engineering exists to prevent. The threshold is reached by raising pressure, lowering temperature, or both, and the demo computes the threshold pressure for its teaching constant. The demo's endpoint states that pressure as the class threshold.

Use and limits. Use this record for hydrogen storage, fuel cells, pipelines, and pressure vessels, and as the interstitial anchor of the whole partition. Do not use the teaching Sievert constant or threshold as measured values for a real host, and do not ignore embrittlement where hydrogen meets stressed steel.
